attempts.raw_response: Unicode employs these terms to designate two distinct diacritical marks that appear in Greek script. The prosgegrammeni, literally "added to the letter," refers to the iota subscript that appears beneath certain vowels in Greek text—a feature inherited from ancient Greek polytonic writing. The ypogegrammeni, meaning "written beneath," similarly describes the iota adscript that historically accompanied long vowels in Greek, though in modern Greek usage these marks have largely fallen out of common practice. Both terms reflect the spatial relationship of the small iota mark relative to the base letter, and their adoption into Unicode's official character names ensures consistent identification across digital text processing and scholarly documentation.

As a phonological phenomenon, the original diphthongs denoted by  are traditionally called "long diphthongs". They existed in the Greek language up into the classical period. From the classical period onwards, they changed to simple vowels (monophthongs), but sometimes continued to be written as diphthongs. In the medieval period, these spellings were replaced by spellings with an iota subscript, to mark former diphthongs which were no longer pronounced. In some English works these are referred to as "improper diphthongs".
